title: Sampled trace GPU utilization investigation (Aug 2025)
content:
Objective:
Run lightweight sampled-trace profiles across realistic sequence-length distributions to understand low-SLO tail latencies and per-SM utilization variance. We want to find if (a) dynamic batching/packing causes kernel launch variance, (b) KV cache eviction patterns produce bursts of memory traffic, or (c) kernel-level divergence / warp serialization is the primary limiter.

Why sampled traces?
- Full timeline captures (Nsight GUI) are heavy and noisy for repeated runs. Sampling with CUPTI + NVTX markers gives us many short traces we can aggregate statistically.
- Helps surface tail events (rare long-running kernels) that amplify p99.

Environment / baseline config:
- Model: open-llm-13B-quant (serving-variant v2.1.3, fused-attention off in this run)
- Hardware: A100-SXM4-80GB, driver 530.41, CUDA 12.1
- Runtime: serving-runtime main @ commit 1a2b3c4 (see PR linked) with dynamic-batcher v3 (packing threshold 80ms)
- Workload: production-like seq distribution sampled from prod traces: 32% <= 128, 48% 129-512, 20% 513-2048
- Repeatable harness: scripts/prof/run_trace_sample.sh (invokes nv-nsight-cu-cli + CUPTI sampling + nvtx markers)

Commands used (representative):
- nv-nsight-cu-cli --session-name sample-run --sample=pc --metrics "sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active" --target-processes all --stop-on-exit 
- python tools/trace_aggregator.py --input-dir /tmp/traces --aggregate-by kernel_name --quantiles 0.5,0.9,0.99 --output traces-summary.csv
- export NVTX_COLOR=1; python examples/run_inference_with_nvtx.py --profile-sampling 1000

Methodology notes (how traces were collected):
- Insert NVTX ranges around: batch_pack, prefetch_kv, attention_forward, kv_cache_insert, postprocess_send
- Enable CUPTI PC-sampling at 1kHz, collect 120s windows across 30 runs to get ~3600 seconds aggregated time
- Use lightweight microbenchmarks for isolated kernels (attention + feedforward) to get roofline points

Key raw observations (aggregated):
- Kernel count per request: median 14, 90th 22, 99th 36 (spikes correspond to cache miss-induced refill paths)
- SM active pct (per-sample): median 58%, 90th 74%, 99th 92%
- Active warps per SM: median 18, 90th 29, 99th 45 (on A100 max is 64 warps/SM)
- Global achieved occupancy (weighted by time): 42%

Lightweight summary table (derived from traces-summary.csv):
Kernel                          | p50 latency | p90 latency | p99 latency | dominant stall reason
--------------------------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|----------------------
attention_forward               | 0.98 ms     | 1.4 ms      | 4.9 ms      | memory (L2) stalls
kv_cache_insert                 | 0.24 ms     | 0.6 ms      | 5.8 ms      | serialization on mutex + memcpy
pack_batches                    | 0.12 ms     | 0.21 ms     | 1.1 ms      | variable input size / launch overhead
ffn_gelu                        | 0.61 ms     | 0.92 ms     | 3.5 ms      | compute (tensor cores not fully utilized)
postprocess_send                | 0.03 ms     | 0.04 ms     | 0.12 ms     | trivial

What stands out (interpretation):
1) High p99s are dominated by a small set of kernels (attention_forward, kv_cache_insert, ffn_gelu) but for different underlying reasons.
2) attention_forward: L2 miss bursts correlate with sequence boundary events (end-of-sequence KV flush). We saw L2 read bandwidth spike in the 99th percentile samples.
3) kv_cache_insert: contention on a host->device memcpy path and a lock around the insertion point — when dynamic packing triggers concurrent insertions we get serialized memcpy windows that block other kernels.
4) ffn_gelu: peak GFLOPS measured in microbenchmarks is 65% of expected theoretical for our tiling; achieved occupancy low because some threadblocks have divergent work (last tile) and launch configuration leaves headroom on SMs.

Per-SM variance insight:
- Sampling shows a subset of SMs (typically 12-18 out of 80 SMs) consistently hitting >90% active warp occupancy while others remain ~30-40%. This indicates persistent imbalance likely coming from block-level scheduling: kernel grid shapes are uneven across batches (due to variable sequence packing).
- When enabling persistent-thread-blocks prototype (local experiment), variance dropped and p99 of attention_forward improved ~18% at the cost of 6% avg latency increase on small batches. Useful tradeoff for p99-sensitive routes.

CUDA graph interactions:
- We tested capturing steady-state graphs for the attention stack. CUDA graphs reduce kernel launch jitter but they are brittle with dynamic pack sizes. For stable-packed routes (fixed sequence bucket), graphs give ~12% p50 improvement and reduce p99 variance by 20%. For mixed-size loads, graph capture fails frequently or requires multi-graph per bucket which increases orchestration complexity.

Quick wins to try (short experiments):
- Remove host-side insertion lock for kv_cache by using per-stream buffers + async memcpy with cudaMemcpyAsync + stream-ordered inserts (low-effort, high-impact).
- Introduce an optional pre-bucket pass that enforces max-packed-size parity (pad small packs to reduce grid imbalance) as an A/B feature for latency-sensitive customers.
- Try 'persistent TB' mode in production for enterprise p99 routes; implement guardrail that disables it for tiny-batch routes.
- Add L2-prefetching hint in attention forward (experiment with __ldg or cuda loads) and measure L2 hit rate change.

Longer investigations / follow-ups:
- Deeper roofline: produce FLOPS vs DRAM bandwidth scatter by kernel, using Nsight compute microbench runs for all kernels. Aim to categorize each kernel as memory/compute/bandwidth limited and produce action matrix.
- End-to-end tail injection test: synthetic injection of cache-eviction events to reproduce rare refills and verify mitigation.
- Explore kernel fusion for attention + kv_insert to reduce memcpy + kernel boundary costs. Evaluate complexity tradeoffs.

Data / artifacts location:
- /tmp/traces/aug2025_sampled/ (compressed .cupti archives) – note these are large; see linked PR for extraction script.
- traces-summary.csv and per-kernel-quantiles/ under the same dir.
- Lightweight visualizations: /artifacts/profiles/aug2025/sm-utilization-violin.png and timeline-sampled-stacks.svg

Open questions / things we couldn't conclude yet:
- Are the L2 miss bursts caused mainly by the model's KV layout (strided accesses) or by concurrent multi-tenant adoption? Need single-tenant isolated runs across two different models to compare.
- Is mutex contention on kv_cache_insert an implementation artifact we can remove with little risk? We need a correctness + race test harness before changing.

Next immediate action items (owners):
- Evan: implement per-stream buffered memcpy for KV insert (prototype branch: pr/evan/kv-async) — due 2025-08-20
- Maria: run microbench roofline suite and collect NVTX-tagged traces for attention + ffn across tiling variants — due 2025-08-18
- Jonas: add A/B flag to runtime to enable persistent-TB for a single route and collect p50/p99 comparisons — due 2025-08-22

Notes-to-self / informal bits:
- Lots of small noisy samples. Don't overfit to one run. Use the aggregator to produce CI-style baseline diffs.
- Add a simple Jasmine/pytest that runs the mutex-free insertion against race-detector in CI.
- Useful Slack threads: #serving-profiles, #infra-gpu (refer to thread ts:1623456789)

Appendix: quick commands to reproduce locally (dev laptop with access to test cluster):
- ./scripts/prof/run_trace_sample.sh --duration 120 --runs 30 --out /tmp/traces/aug2025
- python tools/trace_aggregator.py --input-dir /tmp/traces/aug2025 --aggregate-by kernel_name --quantiles 0.5,0.9,0.99 --output /tmp/traces/aug2025/traces-summary.csv
- nv-nsight-cu-cli --metrics sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active,sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active --sample=pc --target-processes all --session-name quicktest

If we can standardize the sampling harness and add a CI gate for p99 regressions on a small stable dataset, we can get early detection of regressions without heavy Nsight sessions.

-- Aisha
